title: From the end
goal: Unpack long Turkish words and left-branching sentences into natural English, and build them from English.

intro.text: Read Turkish from the end: the last suffix of a word and the main verb of a sentence usually come first in English. Turn participles into relative clauses (**the house where…**), and split a long sentence in two when English would.

vocab.en: the original (of a text): aslından çevirmek, to translate from the original
equivalent (of a word): Türkçe karşılığı, its Turkish equivalent; also reply
fluent, flowing (of a text or a speaker)
predicate, the main verb of a sentence

exercises.question: What is the main statement of *Annemin dün akşam bize anlattığı ev artık yok*?
options: The house is no longer there.
My mother told us something last night.
My mother is no longer there.
We told my mother about a house.

why.1: That is the participle, a description of the house, not the main statement.
why.2: *Annemin* is the subject of the participle *anlattığı*, not of *yok*.
why.3: *Bize* (to us) is who was told; *annemin* is who told.

exercises.explain: The predicate (*yüklem*) is the last word, *yok*; its subject is *ev*. Everything before *ev* describes it: **the house my mother told us about last night**.

exercises.prompt: Have you read the book I lent you?
accept: Sana ödünç verdiğim kitabı okudun mu?
Benim sana ödünç verdiğim kitabı okudun mu
(Benim) size ödünç verdiğim kitabı okudunuz mu
Ödünç verdiğim kitabı [okudun mu|okudunuz mu]

reject.answer: Sana ödünç verdiğim kitap okudun mu?
reject.why: The book is a definite object, so it takes the accusative: *kitabı*.

exercises.explain: The English relative clause moves in front of the noun as a participle: *sana ödünç verdiğim kitap*, with `-DIk` and the possessive of **I**.

exercises.en: Everyone was annoyed that Ali came late.

accept: gelmesi
gelişi

reject.why: As the subject of *kızdırdı*, the event takes `-mA`: *gelmesi* ([B2 unit 4](gp-ma-or-dik)).
The clause is the subject, so it takes no case ending: *gelmesi*.

exercises.hint: The blank is the subject of *kızdırdı*: an event, not a fact you know.
exercises.explain: *Ali'nin geç gelmesi* (Ali's coming late) is the subject; natural English turns it into a clause: **that Ali came late**.

exercises.question: Which English version of *Gelmeniz bizim için çok önemli* sounds most natural?
options: It's very important to us that you come.
Your coming is very important for us.
Coming of you is very important to us.
You come is very important for us.

why.1: Grammatical, but stiff: English prefers a clause here to a verbal noun.
why.2: Not English: the verbal noun can't take **of you**.
why.3: Not English: a clause as subject needs **that**, and usually **it** in front.

exercises.explain: A Turkish verbal noun as subject (*gelmeniz*) usually becomes **it is … that** in English.

exercises.task: Translate into natural English. You may split the sentence.
exercises.source: Geçen yaz, amcamın çocukluğumda bana anlattığı ve kendisinin de yıllardır görmediği köyü sonunda kendi gözlerimle gördüm.
models: Last summer I finally saw with my own eyes the village my uncle told me about when I was a child, a village he himself hadn't seen for years.
Last summer I finally saw the village for myself. My uncle had told me about it when I was a child, though he hadn't seen it himself for years.
checklist: The main statement comes first: **Last summer I finally saw the village**
Each participle becomes a relative clause, or a sentence of its own
*kendisinin de … görmediği*: **he himself hadn't seen** (a pluperfect in English)
*kendi gözlerimle*: **with my own eyes**, or **for myself**

exercises.prompt: She said that she was tired.
accept: Yorgun olduğunu söyledi.
O yorgun olduğunu söyledi
Kendisinin yorgun olduğunu söyledi
Yorgunum dedi
Yorgun olduğunu belirtti
exercises.explain: The English **that** clause becomes a noun clause before the verb: *yorgun olduğunu söyledi*. **She** disappears into the verb ending.

exercises.en: If you translate word for word, the meaning gets lost.
